meta.title: Pretraining and Scaling Laws
meta.thesis: Pretraining and scaling laws explain why larger language models improved: next-token training over massive corpora produces predictable loss trends, but compute-optimal scaling requires balancing parameters, tokens, and data quality.

modules.title: Pretraining teaches broad token prediction
modules.sub: Start with the objective that creates base model capability.
modules.summary: Pretraining is large-scale next-token learning before instruction tuning, preference tuning, or product adaptation.
objectives: Define pretraining in terms of token prediction.
Connect pretraining to later adaptation steps.
Avoid confusing pretraining with RAG or fine-tuning.

blocks.title: The base task is predicting held-out tokens

spans.text: During pretraining, a model sees token sequences and learns to assign high probability to the actual next token. That simple objective, repeated over massive corpora, teaches grammar, facts, code patterns, and many reasoning-like regularities.

Problem anchor: leadership asks why model capability improved so quickly with scale. The answer starts with a broad objective trained over enormous token mixtures, not with a hand-written reasoning engine.

blocks.analogy: Pretraining is like practicing every next move in a huge library of examples before learning a specific job.

spans.text: Sequence: “The refund policy requires an invoice”. The training task asks the model to predict each next token from the previous tokens. The loss is high when the true next token receives low probability, and lower when the model predicts it well.

modules.title: Scaling laws summarize loss trends
modules.sub: Once the objective is clear, connect scale to measured loss.
modules.summary: Scaling laws are empirical relationships showing how loss tends to change with more parameters, data, or compute.
objectives: Define scaling law at a high level.
Avoid treating laws as magic guarantees.

blocks.title: Scale made progress more predictable

spans.text: Scaling laws summarize empirical trends: as model size, data, and compute grow, loss often improves in regular ways over a range. This helped teams plan training runs instead of relying only on trial and error.
The key word is empirical. A scaling law describes observed behavior under assumptions about data, architecture, and training setup. It is not a proof that every downstream task will improve equally.

blocks.analogy: A scaling law is like a fuel-efficiency curve: useful for planning, but not a guarantee for every road.

blocks.title: Toy power-law intuition

spans.text: Run this as a tiny model of the mechanism. The point is to predict behavior before trusting the output.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict whether loss drops linearly or with diminishing returns.
predictThenReveal.answer: It prints decreasing losses with diminishing returns. The exact formula is toy math, but it captures the planning idea: each order of magnitude helps less than the last.

syntax.explains: The small concrete case the example operates on.
The line or function that turns the inputs into behavior.
A visible result so you can check your prediction.

modules.title: Compute budget must be balanced
modules.sub: Loss trends lead to the question of where to spend training compute.
modules.summary: Compute-optimal scaling asks how much budget should go to parameters versus training tokens.
objectives: Explain why bigger models are not always compute-optimal.

blocks.title: Parameters and tokens compete for compute

spans.text: For a fixed training budget, spending everything on more parameters can undertrain the model. Compute-optimal training balances model size and number of training tokens.

The Chinchilla result is commonly summarized as a reminder that data quantity matters alongside parameter count. A smaller model trained on more tokens can beat a larger undertrained model under the same compute budget.

blocks.analogy: Compute allocation is like budgeting a school: more classrooms help only if you also hire teachers and enroll students.

spans.text: Team A trains a very large model for too few tokens. Team B trains a smaller model longer on more data. If Team B reaches lower validation loss for the same compute, the smaller model is the better planning choice.
This does not say small always wins. It says compute should be allocated deliberately.

blocks.title: Check compute balance

options.text: A model that uses RAG at inference time.
A model with many parameters but too few training tokens for the compute budget.

blocks.explanation: Compute-optimal planning balances data and parameters.

modules.title: Data quality shapes what scale buys
modules.sub: After compute allocation, examine the corpus being scaled.
modules.summary: More data helps when it is useful, diverse, deduplicated, and aligned with the target distribution; bad data scales bad behavior.
objectives: Explain why token count is not enough.
Connect pretraining data to downstream capability.

blocks.title: Not all tokens are equally useful

spans.text: Scaling laws often discuss token counts, but the data mixture matters. Duplicates, low-quality text, unsafe content, narrow domains, or missing languages shape what the model learns.
A model trained on more tokens can still perform poorly on a product task if those tokens do not contain the relevant pattern, format, language, or domain.

blocks.analogy: More pages help only if the library contains the subjects you need.

blocks.title: Case study: code model versus support chat

spans.text: A model with strong code pretraining may excel at programming but miss support-tone norms. A model with broad chat and policy examples may answer support questions better even if its headline benchmark is lower.
Use scaling laws carefully; the common mistakes are practical.

items.text: Assuming every benchmark improves at the same rate.
Ignoring data mixture, contamination, and licensing constraints.
Forgetting that downstream prompting, tools, and RAG still matter.
Using loss curves as a substitute for product evals.

modules.title: Scaling laws are planning tools
modules.sub: End by separating pretraining expectations from product guarantees.
modules.summary: Scaling laws help estimate training tradeoffs, but downstream selection still needs task-specific evals, cost analysis, and risk checks.
objectives: Connect model scale to product evaluation.

blocks.title: Loss is not the same as product success

spans.text: Lower pretraining loss often correlates with broader capability, but a product still needs its own evals. The model may be stronger overall and still fail a regulated workflow, a long-context extraction task, or a tool-use policy.
Scaling laws help plan training and model expectations. They do not remove the need for benchmark literacy, red-team checks, latency budgets, and grounded evaluation.

blocks.useWhen: Use scaling-law reasoning to estimate training or model-selection tradeoffs before expensive experiments.
blocks.avoidWhen: Do not use headline scale or lower loss as the only reason to ship a model into a product workflow.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Let scaling laws guide candidates; let task evals decide releases.

blocks.title: Check the lesson
blocks.prompt: What is the safest use of scaling laws?

options.text: Skip evals because bigger models always win.
Plan candidates and budgets, then verify with task-specific evals.
Assume token count matters but data quality never does.

blocks.explanation: Scaling laws inform strategy; product evals decide deployment.
